lead: A graphics display is classed by how much of your field of view it fills. A personal display sits on a desk or in your hand and fills a small angle. A head-mounted display puts a lens and a small panel in front of each eye, so the image fills a large angle and moves with your head. A large-volume display projects on walls or a dome and fills the room. Some syllabi call all of this graphics display and split it into personal, head-mounted and large-volume. The class sets the optics, the pixel size you need and the space you must provide.
prereq: You need: Chapter 3.2 for acuity and field of view.

sections.h3: Personal displays: pixels, distance and angle

blocks.text: A personal graphics display is a screen used by one viewer at a fixed viewing distance: a desk monitor, a stereo monitor, or a phone held in a viewer. The panel has a pixel pitch p, the centre-to-centre distance between pixels, in millimetres. At viewing distance d, one pixel subtends θ ≈ p/d radians. This angular pixel size, not the pixel count, decides whether the eye sees smooth edges. A 0.25 mm pitch at 0.6 m gives θ = 0.25×10⁻³ / 0.60 = 4.2×10⁻⁴ rad ≈ 1.4 arcmin. The eye resolves about 1 arcmin, so the pixel is just visible as a dot; a denser panel or a larger distance hides it.

blocks.where: θ is the angle subtended by one pixel in radians; p is the pixel pitch in metres; d is the viewing distance in metres.

blocks.text: For a phone held 10 cm from a magnifying viewer, the same panel can fill a wide field of view; the lens changes the effective distance and hence the angular size. Personal stereo monitors send different images to the two eyes and are covered in Chapter 3.4. The personal display is cheap and comfortable but fills only the angle of the screen. Move your head and the world does not follow, unless the system adds head tracking.

sections.h3: Head-mounted displays: lens, virtual image and eye box

blocks.text: A head-mounted display (HMD) fixes one small panel per eye, or one panel split between the eyes, a few centimetres from the eye. A magnifying lens makes a virtual image of the panel. The eye focuses on that virtual image, not on the panel, so the panel can be close while the image appears far enough for comfort. The eye is relaxed when focusing at about 1 to 3 m or beyond. A real HMD therefore places its virtual image at that range; a 20 cm image forces strong accommodation and is tiring.

blocks.where: f is the lens focal length in metres, positive for a converging lens; u is the object distance from the lens in metres, negative when the object is on the incident side; v is the image distance in metres, negative for a virtual image on the same side as the object; m is the linear magnification, positive when the image is upright.

blocks.text: The field of view is set by the lens size and the eye distance. The exit pupil is the image of the lens aperture; the eye box is the region in which the eye pupil can sit and still see the full image. Interpupillary distance (IPD) adjustment moves the two eyepieces to match the distance between the user's pupils. Weight matters: a heavy HMD on the head becomes a torque, so the centre of mass should sit close to the face.

An opaque HMD blocks the real world and gives immersive VR. An optical see-through HMD uses a combiner to add computer light to the real view. A video see-through HMD uses cameras and shows the combined video on opaque displays. The last two are AR displays; see Unit 6.

sections.h3: Large-volume displays: CAVE, powerwall, dome and fish-tank

blocks.text: A large-volume display fills a room or a large surface. A CAVE has four to six projection walls, often three walls and the floor, with the viewer inside. Projectors throw images on the walls; software uses the viewer's head position to compute the correct perspective for each wall, so the images join at the edges. Overlapping projector edges are blended in brightness, and the geometry is calibrated, or seams appear. A powerwall is one very large flat screen, often tiled from projectors; it gives a wide field but no floor or side wrap. A dome projects on a curved surface, useful for sky or driving views. Fish-tank VR is the cheap case: a normal monitor with head tracking, so the screen acts as a window into a 3D scene. It gives motion parallax without a room.
The CAVE gives a wide field of view and lets several users stand together. It needs a room, projectors, calibration and dark walls. The wide field is its advantage; the room is its cost.

figure.caption: Light from the microdisplay is magnified by the lens into a virtual image at 20 cm in this teaching case; the eye focuses on that image. A combiner adds a see-through path from the real world to the same eye.

spec.aria: Two light paths: a microdisplay 4 cm behind a lens of focal length 5 cm forms a virtual image 20 cm away and 5 times larger, seen by the eye; a real-world path passes through a combiner to the same eye.

examples.question: A head-mounted display has a lens of focal length 5 cm and its panel 4 cm behind the lens. Find the position of the virtual image, the magnification, and the angle subtended by one 10 micrometre pixel. Take the eye at the lens for the angle estimate.
steps: Use Cartesian signs: light travels left to right, so distances to the right of the lens are positive and to the left are negative. The panel is on the incident side: u = −4 cm. The lens is converging: f = +5 cm.
Apply 1/f = 1/v − 1/u, which rearranges to 1/v = 1/f + 1/u. Then 1/v = 1/5 + 1/(−4) = 0.20 − 0.25 = −0.05 cm⁻¹. So v = −20.0 cm.
The image distance is negative, so the image is virtual and lies on the same side as the panel, 20.0 cm from the lens.
Magnification m = v/u = (−20.0)/(−4.0) = 5.0. The image is upright and 5 times larger than the panel.
The panel pixel is p = 10 μm = 10×10⁻⁶ m. Its image size is 5.0 × 10×10⁻⁶ = 50×10⁻⁶ m.
The image is 20 cm = 0.20 m from the lens. The pixel angle is θ = (50×10⁻⁶)/0.20 = 2.5×10⁻⁴ rad.
Convert to arcminutes: 2.5×10⁻⁴ × (180/π) × 60 = 0.859 arcmin ≈ 0.86 arcmin, near the eye's 1 arcmin acuity limit.
examples.answer: The virtual image is at v = −20.0 cm (20.0 cm from the lens on the panel side), the magnification is m = 5.0, and one 10 μm pixel subtends 2.5×10⁻⁴ rad ≈ 0.86 arcmin. A real HMD would place the virtual image at 1 to 3 m for comfortable focus.
examples.check:
import math
f = 5.0
u = -4.0
v = 1.0 / (1.0/f + 1.0/u)
m = v/u
p = 10e-6
d = abs(v) * 1e-2
p_img = abs(m) * p
theta = p_img / d
arcmin = theta * 180.0/math.pi * 60.0
print(v)
print(m)
print(p_img)
print(theta)
print(arcmin)

traps: Confusing pixel count with resolution: the eye sees pixels per degree, and lens magnification changes the angular pixel size.
Using object and image distances with the wrong sign: measure u and v from the lens, positive to the right; a panel on the left has u negative.
Forgetting that a virtual image at 20 cm is not comfortable: a real HMD places it at 1 to 3 m, which changes the choice of f and u.
Treating exit pupil and eye box as the same: the exit pupil is the image of the aperture; the eye box is the allowed range of pupil positions.
Assuming a CAVE needs no calibration: projector blending and projection geometry must be aligned or seams and distorted edges appear.

quiz.q: Name the three families of graphics displays in this chapter.
quiz.a: Personal displays, head-mounted displays and large-volume displays.

quiz.q: Why does an HMD use a lens instead of placing a panel 1 m from the eye?
quiz.a: The lens creates a virtual image far enough for relaxed focus while the panel stays close. This keeps the device small and light.

quiz.q: A converging lens of focal length 6 cm has its panel 3 cm behind it. Find v and m using the Cartesian sign convention.
quiz.a: u = −3 cm, f = +6 cm. 1/v = 1/6 + 1/(−3) = −1/6 cm⁻¹, so v = −6 cm. m = v/u = (−6)/(−3) = 2. The image is virtual, upright, 6 cm from the lens, and twice as large.

quiz.q: A phone viewer gives a wide field of view but low angular resolution. Explain the tradeoff.
quiz.a: The lens magnifies the phone panel, so the panel fills a wider angle. The same magnification enlarges each pixel's angular size. If the pixel pitch is fixed, the viewer must accept larger pixels per degree, or use a denser panel.

quiz.q: A display has 0.2 mm pixel pitch viewed at 0.5 m. Find the angular pixel size in radians and arcminutes.
quiz.a: θ = 0.2×10⁻³ / 0.5 = 4×10⁻⁴ rad. In arcminutes: 4×10⁻⁴ × (180/π) × 60 = 1.375 arcmin ≈ 1.4 arcmin.

quiz.q: What is the eye box of an HMD?
quiz.a: The eye box is the region in which the eye pupil can sit and still see the full image. It is set by the exit pupil and the optics.

quiz.q: When would you choose a powerwall or fish-tank VR over a CAVE?
quiz.a: Choose a powerwall for a large flat view without needing floor or side walls. Choose fish-tank VR for a cheap desk setup with head-tracked motion parallax. Choose a CAVE when a group needs a wide immersive field and a room is available.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern HMDs add varifocal or multifocal optics to reduce the conflict between focus and stereo depth, and pancake lenses fold the light path to cut weight. Waveguides and microLED panels are moving see-through displays into ordinary glasses. Light-field displays try to reproduce rays rather than a flat virtual image. Search terms: pancake lens, waveguide combiner, varifocal display, light field display, CAVE2.
